newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST-UK poll panel sees 92-seat Labour majority.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-UK poll panel sees 92-seat Labour majority.

text.p: Britain's opposition Labour party is poised to sweep to power with a 92-seat majority, Reuters final survey of leading political experts forecast on Wednesday.
The average of predictions from the 20-strong panel put Tony Blair's Labour party 10 points ahead of John Major's Conservatives.
Labour is set to gather 44 percent of voter support in Thursday's election, the Conservatives 34 percent and Paddy Ashdown's Liberal Democrats 16 percent, the average of the forecasts showed.
"A lot can still happen, but I think Labour is home and dry," said John Benyon, professor of politics at the University of Leicester.

The 92-seat majority is the highest predicted since the survey began in October, but still well short of most public opinion polls, whose results would translate into a Labour majority of 200-plus seats.
The panel, canvassed on April 28, saw on average 375 seats for Labour, 230 for the Conservatives and 26 for the Liberal Democrats with the remainder going to nationalists and other small parties.

Many of the panellists upped their forecasts for Labour support because of continued Conservative bickering and the absence of any sharp narrowing of the Conservative/Labour gap in most opinion polls.

"I thought there would be some significant convergence and the Tories (Conservatives) would catch up. But because of what Edwina Currie said and squabbling in Conservative central office, if anything they are going to lose ground," said Paul Whitely, professor of politics at the University of Sheffield.
Outspoken Conservative MP Currie, in an article in a Sunday newspaper, predicted a 100-strong Labour majority and a bloodbath among her own party's leadership after polling day.

In this survey, Labour's forecast majority has more than doubled since the first survey in October, but the panel remain obstinately less convinced of a Labour landslide than the public polls. The experts said they still expected the Conservative party to claw back some ground in the final 24 hours.

"When it comes to the crunch, some traditional Conservative voters will revert," said Ben Pimlott, professor of politics and contemporary history at Birkbeck College in London. "There is a tendency for Labour to slightly underperform in terms of its actual vote on election day."
But not one of the 20 predicts a last-minute swing to the Conservatives large enough to secure a majority government for John Major.
Even David Carlton -- the odd man out in the panel who until March predicted a nine-seat Conservative majority -- is sticking to his later forecast of a hung parliament.

The panel said the main issues in voters' minds as the campaign entered the home stretch were general competence and trust in the parties, where the sleaze-dogged Conservatives have lost points, as well as management of the economy.

"It's all about image in terms of the ability to manage the economy effectively," said Essex University's Sanders. "The reason the Conservatives are in as much trouble is that they have lost that reputation, while Labour have managed to present themselves as a plausible set of economic managers."
But a simple desire for change could push Labour into government and the Conservatives into a political wilderness.
"People are just fed up now. That's what's going to influence them," said Colin Rallings, professor of politics at the University of Plymouth.
